    57	The problems listed above seem like puzzles. Let’s consider some other problems that seem “deeper” 
    58	or more “general”: 
    59	•	 The “DUH” Problem: Given n, k, and a Turing machine M, is there an input y of size n

    61	•	 The Theorem Problem: Given a mathematical statement and an integer n, is there a 
    62	proof in ZF set theory with at most n symbols?

    67	3.1 The Theorem Problem 
    68	Let’s take a closer look at the Theorem problem. Without the “at most n symbols” constraint, 
    69	would this problem even be computable? 
    70	Claim: If you could solve this problem without that constraint, then you could solve the halting 
    71	problem. 
    72	Proof: Given a Turing machine M, use your algorithm to ﬁnd the answers to the following ques­
    73	tions: 
    74	•	 Is there a proof that M halts? If so, then M halts. 
    75	•	 Is there a proof that M does not halt? If so, then M does not halt. 
    76	If neither proof exists, then we can still conclude that M does not halt. If it did halt, then 
    77	there must be a proof that it does; the most straightforward one being to simulate M until 
    78	it halts. 
    79	Therefore, we can conclude that without the “at most n symbols” constraint, this problem is 
    80	not computable.

    94	4 P and NP 
    95	After 52 years, we still don’t know the answer to G¨odel’s question. But there’s something remarkable 
    96	that we do know. Look again at all of these problems. A priori, one might think brute-force search 
    97	is avoidable for problem X, not for problem Y, etc. But in the 1970s, people realized that in a 
    98	very precise sense, they’re all the same problem. A polynomial-time algorithm for any one of them 
    99	would imply a polynomial-time algorithm for all the rest. And if you could prove that there was 
   100	no polynomial-time algorithm for one of them, that would imply that there is no polynomial-time 
   101	algorithm for all the rest. 
   102	That is the upshot of the theory of NP-completeness, which was invented by Stephen Cook 
   103	and Richard Karp in the US around 1971, and independently Leonid Levin in the USSR. (During 
   104	the Cold War, there were a lot of such independent discoveries.) 
   105	4.1 P and NP 
   106	P is (informally) the class of all problems that have polynomial-time algorithms. For simplicity, 
   107	we focus on decision problems (those having a yes-or-no answer). 
   108	Formally: P is the class of all sets L ⊆ {0, 1}n for which there exists a polynomial-time algorithm 
   109	A such that A(x) = 1 iif x ∈ L. 
   110	NP (Nondeterministic Polynomial-Time) is (informally) the class of all problems for which a so­
   111	lution can be veriﬁed in polynomial time. 
   112	Formally: NP is the class of all sets L ⊆ {0, 1}n for which there exists a polynomial-time Turing 
   113	machine M, and polynomial p, such that ∀x ∈ {0, 1}n : x ∈ L iﬀ ∃y ∈ {0, 1}p(n) s.t. M(x, y) 
   114	accepts (here, x is the instance of the problem and y is some solution to the problem). 
   115	Why is it called “nondeterministic polynomial-time”? It’s a somewhat archaic name, but we’re 
   116	stuck with it now. The original idea was that you would have a polynomial-time Turing machine 
   117	that can make nondeterministic transitions between states, and that accepts if and only if there 
   118	exists a path in the computation tree that causes it to accept. (Nondeterministic Turing machines 
   119	are just like the nondeterministic ﬁnite automata we saw before.) This deﬁnition is equivalent to 
   120	the formal one above. First have the machine guess the solution y, and then check whether y works. 
   121	Since it is a nondeterministic Turing machine, it can try all of the possible y’s at once and ﬁnd the 
   122	answer in polynomial time. 
   123	Question: is P ⊆ N P ? Yes! If someone gives you a solution to a P problem, you can ignore it 
   124	and solve it yourself in NP time.

   146	How can we prove that NP-complete problems even exists? Can we ﬁnd an example of one? 
   147	Consider the “DUH” problem from above: “Given a polynomial-time Turing machine M, ﬁnd 
   148	an input y that causes M(y) to accept.” This problem is NP-complete almost by the deﬁnition of 
   149	NP-complete. 
   150	•	 DUH is in NP: Given a solution y, it is possible to check it in polynomial time simply by 
   151	running M(y) to see if it accepts. 
   152	•	 DUH is NP-hard: Suppose we have an oracle to solve “DUH”. Then given any NP problem, 
   153	by the deﬁnition of NP, there must be some polynomial-time Turing machine M �(x, y) for 
   154	verifying a claimed solution y. So just ask the oracle whether there exists a y that causes M 
   155	to accept (having hardwired the input x into the description of M).

   157	exist. That is almost tautological. Their real achievement was to show that many natural problems

   164	4.4 Proving a problem is NP-complete 
   165	To show a given problem L is NP-complete, you only have to do two things: 
   166	1. Show L ∈ NP.

   168	is NP-hard, since it must be at least as hard as K for K to reduce to L. 
   169	5 The Cook-Levin Theorem 
   170	Consider another problem: SAT (for Satisﬁability). Given an arbitrary Boolean formula (in propo­
   171	sitional logic), is there any way of setting the variables so that the formula evaluates to TRUE? 
   172	Theorem. SAT is a NP-complete problem.

   174	of arguments, plug them into the equation and see if it evaluates to TRUE.

   176	hard. We know DUH is NP-complete, so let’s reduce DUH to SAT. In other words: given some 
   177	arbitrary polynomial-time Turing machine M, we need to create a Boolean formula F , which will 
   178	be satisﬁable if and only if theres an input y that causes M to accept. And the translation process

    12	While Cook and Levin showed that SAT is NP-complete, Richard Karp showed in 1972 that NP-completeness is not just an isolated phenomenon.     16	2. Proof Strategy
    17	The overall proof strategy relies on the transitivity of polynomial-time many-one reductions.
    18	Step 1: Start with a known NP-complete problem. Karp started with SAT (which was proven NP-complete by Cook).
    19	Step 2: Reduce SAT to 3SAT.
    20	Step 3: Build a tree of reductions. For example, reduce 3SAT to Clique, then Clique to Vertex Cover, then Vertex Cover to Hamiltonian Cycle, etc.

    27	To reduce 3SAT to Clique, we construct a graph from a 3CNF formula.
    28	- Nodes: Create a node for every literal in every clause. If there are k clauses, there are 3k nodes.
    29	- Edges: Connect two nodes if they are in DIFFERENT clauses AND they are logically consistent (i.e., they are not a variable and its negation).

    33	This is a straightforward graph complement reduction.
    34	- Reduction: A graph G has a clique of size k if and only if its complement graph G' has a vertex cover of size |V| - k.

    36	3.3. Directed Hamiltonian Cycle to Undirected Hamiltonian Cycle
    37	- Reduction: Expand each node into three nodes (in, mid, out) to force the undirected cycle to traverse the nodes in the same direction as the directed edges.
